utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Today we'll start with the videolink testimony. And I was informed that we have a good connection with Sarajevo. The Defence calls as its next witness Velimir Radojevic, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, you hear me in a language you understand? I cannot hear your answer. I now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now also can hear you, Mr. Radojevic. Can you also see us on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see you. I can see you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, before giving testimony before the Tribunal, before this Chamber, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the representative of the Registry. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration. Please, stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please, be seated. Mr. Radojevic, you will first be examined by counsel for the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radojevic.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, we would first of all like you to introduce yourself. Could you tell us where you lived in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I lived in part of Sarajevo in Blazuj in the municipality of Ilidza. I worked for the power lines. It was a company, a power line company --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Radojevic. Could you please speak slowly because the interpreter has to interpret what you are saying. Could you just tell us briefly, you lived in part of Sarajevo in the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Blazuj settlement, the Blazuj neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I assumed that this was Mr. Radojevic. It is not yet his testimony. Perhaps we should do that right at the beginning that you ask for this personal details. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, could you first of all tell us when you were born and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of October, 1949 in Bilcici, the municipality of Rogatica in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radojevic. Mr. Radojevic, can you tell us your father's name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Milos.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, you told us that you lived in the municipality of Ilidza. Since when have you lived in that municipality? Since when have you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since 1974 right up until the Dayton Agreement in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, you told us that you worked for Energoinvest company?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the long distance power line company. It's the company for constructing such long distance power lines in Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, can you tell us what you are by profession?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am a qualified locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, what sort of work and work tasks did you have to carry out in your company?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a brigadier in the group for installing the long distance power lines and for installing of vertical transport systems and ski lifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, in 1992, we will be talking about September of 1992, were you employed in the company you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in Elektroprenos in the Ilidza branch. That's where I was employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, when you said that you had work obligations to carry out there, can you tell us which organ obliged you, so to speak, to carry out these duties?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the Municipal Assembly or the president of the municipality of Ilidza who made me do this, who gave me this obligation because I was the only person in that area, the only Serbian who was qualified to carry out that work. And my task was to form a group to maintain the long distance power lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you go into the details about the forming of this team, what was the reason for forming the team? Can you tell us whether you had any duties in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you told us that you formed a commission, can you tell us at what level this commission was formed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not a commission, a team for maintaining the long distance power line, I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At what level was that team formed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I found three men who worked with me; one was from Hadzici, one from Blazuj -- two were from Blazuj. After that, in June, a colleague from Zenica came and he joined us and a fourth colleague or rather a fifth colleague who was also from Hadzici and worked with us before the war. These men helped with the installation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, the team that was formed, what duties did that team have?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: My team's duties were to repair, carry out all repairs of the long distance power line in the area of the so-called Sarajevsko Romanijski Plateau. That's where there would be faults because of the conflict. That's where the system would break down, because of the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you had to repair the long distance power line in the Sarajevsko Romanijski plateau, could you tell us, before the conflict broke out, before the war broke out in the area of the town of Sarajevo, how was the town of Sarajevo supplied with electricity? Where were their long distance power lines for supplying the town of Sarajevo with electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I will put this in the correct chronological order, but it goes from the power station Jablanica, through the Blazuj electricity station and then from the power plant Piva through the electricity station in Lukavica and Reljevo and then through the Reljevo station from the direction of Mostar, there was Ilidza and from the direction of Tuzla and the Vogosca electricity station which received electricity from the Visegrad power station. These electricity stations were at the periphery of the town. They were 400 watts strong, 110 and 35. These were electricity stations from which the electricity went into the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, could you please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask the -- there seems to be a microphone switched on somewhere. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, when you said that you were in a team which carried out repairs on the long distance power line, repairs which were required and repairs which were carried out during the war, can you tell us in which part of the Sarajevo Romanija plateau, as you call it, in which part of this plateau would there be repairs as a result of the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The most frequent faults happened in the Kljuc area between Rogatica and Reljevo. Then in part of Vogosca which is between Kiseljak and Reljevo and Blazuj. That is the long distance power line from Kakanj to Reljevo and there was faults in part of Zenica. In the direction of Visegrad and Rudo the columns would be destroyed. The electricity would go towards Serbia so that the Visegrad power plant could work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, when you went to carry out repairs you have mentioned locations. On that occasion did you go with your team alone or was it necessary for you to be escorted?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We also went with an UNPROFOR escort and a day or two before we would go to the site where there were faults, we would agree on a certain site that UNPROFOR would designate. We would agree that a colleague from the Muslim side and I should agree how to enter the site and how to carry out the repairs there, how to carry out the repairs of the fault on the long distance power line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have now answered -- you have now said that you went to carry out repairs with an UNPROFOR escort and after having consulted a colleague on the Muslim side. Have I understood your answer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But in the area of the town of Sarajevo, but to carry out repairs outside the town in Visegrad, in the direction of Visegrad, I would go there on my own with my team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I have understood you correctly, all the repairs that were carried out in the town of Sarajevo, whenever you went to carry out these repairs, a mixed team, so to speak, went. You would go with UNPROFOR escort. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When a mixed team would go to these sites to carry out repairs, are you telling us that you also went to the part of the town of Sarajevo which was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and the part of the city of Sarajevo which was under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that that was the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... both areas, under control of both parties, that's how I understand the question. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, when you went to carry out repairs on the site on the part that was under the control of the BH Army, you will first answer this part of the question: Can you tell us which areas were most exposed to faults, where were the most faults?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in the area of Zuc Toka Donji [phoen] and the area behind the Zrak factory. These two sites. I went to those two sites with a colleague of mine when repairs had to be carried out because the BH Army thought that Republika Srpska Army would shell that area when they were -- when repairs were being carried out. But that didn't happen. We managed to repair that line successfully. And I was even congratulated by the local population after having carried out the repairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that many repairs had to be carried out in the area of Zuc and the Zrak factory, can you tell us how often you would go to those areas to carry out repairs?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Each time an offensive was launched in the Zuc area, there would be faults because the long distance power station which supplied the transformer station from Reljevo and the transformer station from Zuc and Potok and the transformer station in Zuc and Reljevo they were between the firing lines. And whenever there was a fighting the lines would be broken and we would have to go and carry out the repairs. But as far as the town is concerned, I was in the centre of the town twice. In Buca and Potok on both occasions. That's behind Zrak factory and in Mali Zuc that's what it is called over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojevic, when you went to carry out these repairs, were UNPROFOR members with you on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and I am talking about the period September 1992 and August 1994, about that period, from September 1992 to August 1994, when during this period, if you can tell us this on the basis of your personal knowledge, when were the repairs that you carried out actually carried out? Can you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any notes -- I don't have the notes that I had with me. I can't tell you exactly, but there were faults so frequently during that period because there were offensives, there was shooting. And we would repair the power line on one day and the following day there would no longer be any electricity. In the part under the control of the Republika Srpska or under the control of the BH Army didn't have electricity either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive any English translation. Is this problem solved? Could you please speak some words in B/C/S, Ms. Pilipovic, so that we can see whether we receive a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, you hear me?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question was, when you went to carry out repairs, and now we are speaking about the repairs that you carried out in the part of the city controlled under the BH Army. When a pylon on Zuc was damaged and when you went to carry out repairs, what parts of the city would be without electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If there was damage on any part of pylon that goes around over Zuc or whether it's Vogosca, Velesici, Reljevo, or Buca Potok the entire city would be without electricity because in the period of war, the close centre of Sarajevo would get electricity from these two directions, from Reljevo towards Buca Potok and Velesici so if there was any breakdown in the pylon connection, then the Buca Potok transformer station wouldn't get any power either, and I would then have to list any other locations that would be in the area under the control of the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I have understood you correctly, when damage occurred on the long distance power line in Buca or in the area of the Zrak factory or in the area of Buca Potok, then parts of the city under the control of the BH Army would have no electricity as well as the parts of the city under the control of the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us just from based on your personal experience during this period, how many days or how many hours during a month or a year that parts of the city would have no electricity supply? Do you think you could answer that in general?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't -- I can just tell you in general. In 1993, but I am not quite sure, parts of the city of Sarajevo, close city centre, including the part of the Serb Sarajevo didn't have electricity for three months. The reason was the breakdown on the long distance power line between Visegrad, Kakanj and Reljevo. Because there was a long distance line between Kakanj and Reljevo that was broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you told us that there was a period where for three months there was no electricity supplied in the parts of the city also under the control of the BH Army and under the control of the Republika Srpska Army, can you tell us, what were the parts of town during those three months that you mentioned had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to me, the entire -- in my opinion, the entire city of Sarajevo. When we repaired Visegrad, Vogosca lines, we managed to get supply for Vogosca. So two or three days later there was shelling so the pylon fell again. And practically for three months literally nobody had electricity, although we did make an effort to get electricity supply as much as we could for the parts of Sarajevo that we were able to get electricity supply for.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now that you have told us the entire city of Sarajevo had no electricity supply, are you saying to us that also the part of the city under the control of the BH Army as well as the part of the city under the Republika Srpska Army, had no electricity for three months; is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the period of time which is relevant for us, that is from September 1992 until August 1994, can you tell us approximately when between in this period were these three months? Was this in 1993 or was this from 1992, September 1992, when the entire city of Sarajevo had no electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I think that that was in 1993, but I can't tell you for sure because I don't have my agenda or notes because I didn't expect you to ask me this question. UNPROFOR has all the records when things happened and when things were repaired, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have now explained to us how during the period of war, how this mixed team functioned with UNPROFOR escort, and how they carried out repairs to electricity equipment in certain parts of town. Did I understand you correctly, that mixed teams went out to carry out repairs also in those parts of town that were under the control of the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: All our missions with UNPROFOR in mixed teams that we carried out, we carried out in the territory under the control of the Republika Srpska as well as under the control of the BH Army, although never did it happen that entire teams went to the parts of the town controlled by the BH Army. But I went with a colleague of mine from Sarajevo. I waited at the checkpoint in Reljevo and then we would go from Reljevo to Zuc or to Golo Brdo or from the direction of Vogosca, Vogosca, depending on where the damage was, and depending on which road we had to take. In that, we had to have the agreement of local commanders and they didn't cause any trouble, as far as the entering the area that needed to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you got agreement -- you got guarantees from local commanders, can you tell us and can you answer, was it always the case that you got guarantees from local commanders on the Muslim side and on the Serb side when you carried out repairs?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I ensured this to be acquired from local Serb commanders, where my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Got them from Muslim commander. When we got in the direction of Vogosca, one of the workers from the Muslim teams would be on the Muslim line with a radio station. He would be in connection with me. And he would then say, you can go, everything has been agreed, no problem. This is how we went across one set of trenches and other set of trenches and this is how we carried out repairs on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer, in which way the UNPROFOR members were informed, and did they also need a guarantee to be escorting you on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, UNPROFOR had an engineering unit which was located in the PTT engineering. And their task was to provide workers to carry out repairs to pylons, long distance power lines and so on. And for all the damage in the city, this was done by the French Army and they needed through the connection with the Serb and the Muslim side, then they would agree that there should be no fire. And then we would go out with them to the scene, and they were, for us, this military guarantee. They guaranteed safety for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us in every situation when you went to carry out repairs as part of the mixed team escorted by UNPROFOR, were you always able to carry out repairs in security, in safety?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not. On one occasion in the Golo Brdo area, we went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the French Battalion by Reljevo line, we got to the Serb Army lines. We were told there was no problem, you can work. We went into the area of repair or area of the damage. These were lines where the demarcation lines were 100 metres, one from each other. When we got in and when the mixed team got in, when the French soldiers got in, then fire was opened from the Muslim side. Perhaps somebody who didn't know that the repairs were going to be done, firing started. There was shooting. And for about an hour and a half, we were literally between two fires, both us and the French soldiers. And one of the French soldiers was wounded and then we went to one or two days later, and everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you told us about this incident which took place with the presence of UNPROFOR, can you tell us, when did this take place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer me the question, when was this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date because I told you, I didn't bring anything with me as far as the notes were concerned. I didn't know I would be able to. So I wouldn't be able to tell you all the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which year that was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that was in 1993. I remember that was Major Roquitat [phoen] who led the French.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly you said a name of the French major who escorted this mission?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us -- repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was a major, that was his rank, and his name was Roquitat, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you tell us about the interventions that came as a consequence of war operations, you told us that some of the demarcation lines were only 100 metres away from each other. Can you tell us, for all the areas that you went to where were the damages? When I say "where" were they in the vicinity of the demarcation lines, or were they in certain areas outside of the area of demarcation lines?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, damages occurred between demarcation lines, sometimes behind lines. If there was a pylon there, so maybe a shrapnel or a bullet would cut the cable, and that's how then there would be the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain, can you answer, is it possible that in some parts of the city there would be electricity, and that in other parts of the city, there would be no electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was not nothing to do with us. If all the damage -- if all the damage was repaired and in the Buca Potok and Velesici got their electricity supply, and everything depended of electricity supply of Bosnia-Herzegovina to distribute it as it should be distributed to the users. Because during the war, most of the time there was electricity supply for the entire city of Sarajevo including both parts, the Muslim and the Serb. There was 60 to 65 megawatts, that was a minimum to get electricity from the entire city for all the users to have electricity supply normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that that would be a reason why in certain parts of the city there would be electricity supply and some other parts there would be no electricity supply because of very poor voltage?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be because of that. But of course the electricity would be given to -- as we all know, it would be distributed to what was considered to be priorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that it was normal to get electricity supply to priorities, could you tell us, how was it possible to provide electricity for the so-called priorities? Is that possible and how?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible because in every equipment, in every transformer station, they have switches and all different kinds of equipment and switches. And through them, you get electricity supply to the pylon, to the long distance line, that would get a supply for a certain area. And then there we be all go to a distributor transformer station which in the same way they would then distribute the electricity supply for one area or another area and so on. Again, there was a system of switches, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now that you have explained to us that there would be -- there would be electricity provided for the so-called priorities, can you tell us, in war, who had the right, if you know, to decide on priorities?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who had the right, but I think humane right would be for priority to go to hospitals, that they would get electricity supply. And I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally have any knowledge that in the part of the city that was under the control of the BH Army, and the BH Army was able to provide or to decide on priorities for parts of the units that were included in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no information, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. It is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a leading question, Ms. Pilipovic, so would you please reformulate the question. And keep in mind the answers--

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with the witness saying he has no information. So if it would come to speculation, then it might not assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you told us with respect to priorities -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had no information as to who was able to supply electricity for the so-called priorities. Did you ever, and when, did you have any information as to parts of the city under the control of either side, of either army, that the question of priorities was under the control of the army? Do you have any such knowledge or information?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge. But at that time anybody could have come with weapons and say to the duty electrician in the transformer station, "switch this on." And even if that didn't happen, any commander could have asked for their own unit to have electricity supplied. This was possible, but I have no knowledge or information that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you were telling us about the control, about the repairs to electricity equipment in the city of Sarajevo, can you tell us whether when electricity was cut in certain parts of town, could that then cause that the water supply is cut? Is the electricity supply and water supply connected somehow? Do you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can explain as much as I know. For instance, Bacevo source at the Vrelo Bosne it cannot work without the electricity, because this source is on a flat land, and from that source, you cannot get water to go to the -- through the pump to the users. Also, in another location, you -- also in Tilava you also need a pump, and in other parts of the city of Sarajevo, for instance, towards Mount Jahorina I have no information, so I can't give you any information. But for these two sources that I mentioned, you can't even get water supply to Ilidza, or they are actually located in Ilidza because it is a flat land so they can't work without pumps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, the source Bacevo in the Ilidza municipality cannot supply water for Ilidza municipality without electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It cannot because pumps cannot work that send water on to the users, to the consumers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you personally tell us whether there were periods of time from 1992, from September 1992 until August 1994, when there was no electricity in certain parts of town as a result of no electricity, and therefore, Bacevo source couldn't work?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, electricity, there would be no electricity in Ilidza and in Blazuj and then there would be no water -- because there was no water because there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us there was no water in Ilidza, can you tell us were these certain periods of time when there was no water and how long would this go on for?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because water supply wasn't my area and I don't know for sure. But I think I had -- they had generators and they were able to use generators. But I can't tell you for sure because I was really -- my area of expertise were pylons to get them back up and to get the long distance power lines working, to get the electricity supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When Bacevo source did not work, when you said there was no electricity, Bacevo source couldn't work and there would be no water in Ilidza, can you tell us whether at that time in certain parts of town of Sarajevo under the control of the BH Army there was no water as well?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's true. They didn't have water, but there were parts, as far as I know, as far as I can say, from those sources that came from the sources where there was a free fall of water. I am not quite sure which ones they are. But it can be from Bascarsija and those from Jagomir and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us there was sources in Bascarsija and Jagomir, can you tell us these sources, in your opinion, through which it was possible to get water supply into the city, under whose control were they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think they were under the control of the BH Army. I don't know what exactly the source is called over there behind but I guess it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you answered in the question with respect to the causes for lack of electricity in parts of Sarajevo and certain parts in the entire city of Sarajevo and for the shortage of water in conditions of war which were then prevalent, was it possible for one of the sides -- and here we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mean the side which had under its control part of the Sarajevo -- one part that was under the control of the Republika Srpska and one under the BH Army, was it possible for them to influence the distribution of electricity and water in the city? Do you know about electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were not able to influence because if we would switch on the electricity in any transformer station in the city, that was done by day dispatchers and that was done by their people in the transformer stations. We were not able to influence how they would distribute their electricity because that was -- that was their area. That was their business.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in Sarajevo, that is, in the entire city of Sarajevo on both sides, would electricity be cut, there would be no electricity because both sides switched electricity supply off?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. The only reason this happened is because of the damage of the breakdown of the faults on the pylons, on the long distance power lines

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the period from September 1992 until August 1994, did you at any time give certain statements to the media regarding the damage, the cause of the damage, and the electricity shortage?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I gave a statement following my wounding in Zuc. I gave a statement after we repaired the pylon in Vogosca. I think that was in 1994, either in June or July. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is the period we are talking about in 1992, 1993, when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you for sure, but I can explain how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, I understand that you would like to play the videotape. I am informed that the quality of the view in Sarajevo might be less than it is here. But let's try and see what happens. Perhaps you specifically ask the witness whether the picture on the screen is clear enough to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I please have the exhibit number of the tape and which is the corresponding transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D348/8. D348/8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Serbian Sarajevo zone is once again without electric power. Can you tell us what are the problems involved? There was no Military activities in this area. I have to say that there was a problem. I have been wounded when I went out with the crew to repair the high tension power line Reljevo-Buca Potok. We went there regularly accompanied by UNPROFOR and met the Muslim Side repair crew, to agree on how the work is to be done. As I Was taking my men to the power line, a grenade exploded. I really Don't know what type it was, but it fell about three or four Metres away from me. I was wounded in my lower legs. The Following day, my team went out to repair that line. It was a Mixed team, naturally, and included our men and Muslims, together With an UNPROFOR escorts. We were requested to go out on the Field on Sunday, but without UNPROFOR the Elektroprenos from Republika Srpska did not go out. It was prepared to go out for Repairs today, but the works were postponed today. Yesterday, Namely Sunday, there was a power cut in the afternoon around 3.00 P.m. I don't know why. A power failure was announced and I heard About this this morning on the radio. I heard that one of the Breakdowns was known and the other one was unexplained. We do not know whether lines have been interrupted somewhere Between the Croatian Muslim lines. It has already happened Several times that the zones of Ilidza and Hadzici have been left In the dark due to the interruptions of power lines in the city. I personally disprove of that because the men that work with me Are more than willing to go out for repairs not only in daytime, But at night too if need, in a mixed team and with an UNPROFOR Escort to repair all that is necessary provided that fair honest Treatment is ensured. The order should be given, regardless of Which army is involved, that civilians and workers involved in Humanitarian missions should not be shot at. So that's what Happened to me again. Does this mean that because of the interruption of the power line From Vogosca to Sarajevo, the Muslims cut off electricity to this Part of Serbian Sarajevo? I can't say that that is what happened with certainty. There are Some indications that the power line is functioning correctly, but As we did not go out to carry out repairs yesterday, the power Line has simply been shut down. This will be cleared up today and our liaison officers and Engineers who work in the UNPROFOR engineering sector will be Having a meeting today at 1.00 p.m. and they will agree on repair Crews that have to be sent out to repair the high tension power Line. Also because on Saturday, as a result of military activity, The power line in Vogosca-Velisici which used to supply the Priority users in Sarajevo. This is a power line bringing power From Serbia and it is a well known fact. About 2 to 3 megawatts Were also directed to Grbavica. Grbavica has been left without Electricity to. Thank you. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you able to recognise the video that we have just seen? Mr. Radojevic, can you hear me? Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we get no response, I take it that the witness cannot hear you. Could the technicians please try to find out why the witness doesn't receive any sound. Could you please try it again, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we will get a sign from the technicians when the sound connection, the audio connection is in effect again. Yes. If no one speaks, then we cannot test whether it works. Do you hear me again, Mr. Radojevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see whether we can reschedule then this morning and have two breaks of the same length. That would mean that we have a break now for 25 minutes, and that we will have a second break later on also of 25 minutes. We adjourn until 25 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, could you please speak a few words so that we can see whether we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear you clearly. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we had a look at a video before the break.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the video?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the video that we had a look at, were you being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one day after I had been wounded in Zuc when carrying out repairs on the long distance power line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did this video perhaps remind you of that period of time, the season or the year?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't because I also had a medical certificate at home and all the details, but I didn't think it was necessary to bring any papers with me. I hadn't been informed, otherwise I would have provided you with detailed information. If necessary, I can fax this to the Defence after this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in your interview, you told us what the reason of the damage was when electricity was being provided to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that the reason for which the electricity supply was cut off in Hadzici in Ilidza, do you remember mentioning the reason?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I said that, but I know that the long distance power line in that area, I think it's between Stubovo [phoen] between the 11th and 12th between Reljevo and Buca Potok. I think there was damage in one of the power lines and we went to carry out repairs. That night there was fighting in that area. We arrived up there. A Muslim team arrived from its side and I came from Reljevo with my team. We contacted each other via radio link. The line was very close, 50 to 70 metres away, perhaps. No more than that. I went to the part where the Army of Republika Srpska was and reached the road where I met my colleagues on the other side. Muradif Sabanovi, a liaison officer was there, a liaison officer with UNPROFOR on behalf of Electroprevrida of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were two other men who agreed on how we should proceed, how we should work. I said, "Saban," that's what we called him, "you pull a line through and my installers will bring other equipment. We will repair this quickly. And since UNPROFOR carriers are with you, you can sort that out quickly and then we will withdraw as quickly as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible, because as you can see, it is very dangerous here."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you slow down, please. We will get to that. But could you finish what you were saying, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: After the agreement, I went to my team which was on the left side to the left of me. I don't know from which position, a rifle launch grenade was fired. It hit a log, a tree that had been destroyed and the fragments of the shell hit the bush and I was hit by fragments of the shell in the left leg and shoulder. At the time I didn't feel any pain. I went down to the team and told them what had happened. I said, "Let's finish the job." Huso had asked me whether I had been wounded. I said, "Veljo," that's his nickname, I said, "No, let's finish this job and then let's go."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, sir, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Radojevic, for a clarification. What exactly was the distance between you and the shell that was falling close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the shell and myself the distance was about 2 to 3 metres. The shell fell 2 to 3 metres from me. It hit a tree. I was protected by a tree which was between me and the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked this, Ms. Pilipovic, because there was a difference in the interpretation from the booth and from what we read in the transcript of the video. It was interpreted as 3 to 4 feet, where it seems to be a couple of metres, rather than a couple of feet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, you told us that on that day when you were carrying out repairs with your team and with an UNPROFOR escort, you said that on that day you were wounded. You said that you didn't know the location, but can you tell us under whose control the area was? Do you know from which side the rifle launched grenade was fired?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was fired from the Muslim side. And at that point I saw that the command of the line, an officer's whose name I don't know, and two or three other men with him, I saw that by the road near the line, they ran down to where the weapon was fired from to see who it was. Later I was told that the rifle launch grenade was accidentally fired, that the man wasn't aware of what he should do. But what happened, happened, that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you went to carry out repairs with an UNPROFOR escort, did you pass through certain parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I went to carry out repairs in Buca Potok, UNPROFOR was waiting for me at a checkpoint in Reljevo. I went from the direction of Reljevo through Brijesce, as far as Buca Potok. And that's where I carried out repairs. And I used the same route to return because that is the only checkpoint through which we could pass was through there. The Reljevo checkpoint was the only checkpoint that engineers could pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, when you went to the lines to carry out repairs, you as a team, I am referring to the entire team, the mixed team, did you have certain identification signs that showed that you were a team involved in carrying out repairs?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have markings, identification signs of any kind. We had various sorts of clothing. Some people were wearing working clothes. Some people were wearing jeans. It depended on what the people had. Although, at meetings with UNPROFOR when we were arranging how to carry out work at various sites, I asked them to allow us to carry white flags on the cars to mark the cars with these white flags and with certain markings. But at the time we didn't receive permission to do so, see we went to carry out the repairs without any particular identification marks, apart from the fact that the UN vehicles were identifiable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you carried out repairs in Buca Potok, and in Buca Potok, was there a location that you could identify for us? Was there a particular location where you could mention, a particular location where you carried out repairs?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind the Zrak factory. That's where the Odzakovici settlement is located. It's called in that way because of surname of the people who live there. Two of us turned up there in order to ensure that there would be no shooting from Republika Srpska Army. This never happened in any case. But we turned up to help. I worked on one pylon. I went down to the team. I was met by someone in civilian clothing who had identification papers. He said, "Hello," and he asked, "Do you have more work to do?" I said, "We're coming to an end." I said, "I am the chief of the security --" he said, "I am the chief of security. My police are providing security and is insuring that the people should not be afraid and insuring that nothing should happen to them."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you to reply slowly. Just speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were telling us that you went to carry out repairs in the Buca Potok area behind the Zrak factory, do you know whether that factory during the time of the conflict, do you know whether that factory produced anything? Do you have any personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. Because I couldn't have found this out from anyone. I only went there to carry out repairs on the power line and to fix things.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you tell us whether you as a team, you personally, at any time were you under any commands of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally and my team, we were never at any time under the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and we didn't receive any orders from them of any kind with regard to what we should do and with regard to how we should do that. Any technical agreements with regard to carrying out repairs would be agreed by me with my colleagues on the Muslim side. And when there was damage in the territory under the control of the Republika Srpska Army, I would personally make the plans and my colleagues from the team, and we would go into the field to carry out those repairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in the video that we saw, at one point you claimed that electricity for certain parts of the town that the electricity supply to certain parts of the town came from Serbia too. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. But I will clarify this matter. I will clarify how the electricity was obtained from Serbia. In order for the power station in Visegrad to work, it had to consume at least 50 megawatts. This was the minimum. Without this minimum, it wasn't able to function. So the power line, Visegrad, Rudo, Bijeljina through that power line, we would send electricity to Serbia. But that electricity was only being taken to Republika Srpska and Bijeljina Krajina because they didn't have enough electricity. And without such a system, the power station in Visegrad wouldn't have been able to function because it needed to have this technical minimum, as far as consumption is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now that you have clarified how the electricity was supplied through the power plant in Visegrad, can you tell us whether damage to one of the power plants could cause the electricity to be cut off in Sarajevo? And we are talking about power plants.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Any sort of damage to the power plant can result in a cut -- in the electricity being cut off in Sarajevo, whether it is from Jablanica and Kakanj, through the Kakanj-Reljevo place, but it doesn't matter where it comes from. In all cases, the electricity supply can be cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know what the reason for which the electricity supply to the city was cut off was that there was damage to the Jablanica power station, the Jablanica-Kakanj hydroelectric power station? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember this because of the period. But whenever the Kakanj-Reljevo power station was faulty, that was a reason for why the Serbian part of Sarajevo and the strict centre of Sarajevo didn't have any electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the Jablanica hydroelectric power station, can you tell us how far it is from the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it is about 60 kilometers from the town, but at the beginning of the conflict the Jablanica one power line and the Jablanica two power line, which are 110 kilowatt power lines, and linked to the Blazuj transformer station or rather to Sarajevo 1 in part of the municipality of Hadzici and between Pozderici because of shells they were damaged, pylons were damaged and they weren't functioning right up until the end of the war. So that the Blazuj transformer station didn't have any supply. Didn't receive anything from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, have I understood you correctly that when you say there was damage to those power lines, was Hadzici an area which didn't have any electricity for a long period of time? Was that one of the reasons why Hadzici or Blazuj didn't have any electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally because the only alternative source of electricity was the Jablanica-Kakanj power line and the Visegrad Vogosca power line. So if any power line was not functioning, we would remain without electricity in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you said that one of the reasons -- when you said that one of the reasons for electricity in Sarajevo was low voltage, was this manifest in parts of the town to a greater or lesser extent? Did some parts of the city because of low voltage, did some parts of the city remain without electricity and which parts were concerned?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably. But that was because of a centre in Bosnia-Herzegovina which -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for one clarification, Mr. Radojevic. Two times Ms. Pilipovic has asked you about low voltage. What I heard as a matter of fact is low number of megawatts. Is it the voltage or is it the wattage that caused the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem was the small -- the low number of megawatts. The dispatching centres in the town of Sarajevo had to decide how to distribute it and how to decide on the amount of electricity they would provide to various consumers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is my understanding right that voltage is a totally different thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood that well. If you have a sufficient amount of megawatts, then the power is a sufficient, but if you don't, then you don't have sufficient power. So if the water is passing through a pipe, and we have to distribute it to 150 households, then that's not possible. There is water, but the capacity is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, did I understand you correctly that it was to do with the dispatching centre where these stations existed in certain parts of town, where it was their area of expertise that certain parts of the city could be supplied with electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly correct. And even today in peacetime, dispatchers are those who decide from where and where the electricity is going to go, from which part of the town to which part of the town and which switches will be used to switch on the electricity. Because the dispatchers are the basic field for the supply of electricity. They are the ones who will make sure that there is no problem with the electricity supply, that there is no breakdown, so that I didn't go into to many technical details. So if they get a message, what they do is they get messages through those duty electricians and transformers stations about electricity supply and who will get what.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no further questions. Let me just confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, the area of Jablanica and Kakanj, can you tell us under whose control was it, under the control of which arm?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Jablanica was under the control of the BH Army, and Kakanj was as well also under the control of the BH Army, as far as I know. That doesn't have to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojevic, you will now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you be able to say as to how many substations supplied electricity to Sarajevo prior to the outbreak of the war? And I am referring to the period February, March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I will be able to give you the exact number, but I will try to list them by their names. Blazuj transformer station; Sarajevo one; Reljevo, Sarajevo 10; Vogosca, Sarajevo 4; Velesici transformer station, Sarajevo 2; Buca Potok transformer station; Nedzarici transformer station; Hrasnica transformer station; Lukavica transformer station; Otoka transformer station; Skenderija transformer station; and Kosevo transform station. At this very moment I wouldn't be able to list any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, sir, would you agree that there were about 10 to 12 substations supplying power to Sarajevo prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count them, but I would agree. If you counted while I was listing the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And sir would you be able to say during the period of the conflict, and I am specifically referring to the period September 1992 to August 1994, how many substations supplied power to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Buca Potok transformer station and Velesici transformer station, on the side of the control of the BH Army. And the Blazuj, Reljevo, and Vogosca on the area under the control of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I suggest to you, sir, that during the period of conflict, that is of the period September 1992 to August 1994, the main substation that supplied power to Sarajevo was Buca Potok? Pardon the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would agree because from the direction of Reljevo, electricity went to Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the entire consumption of power that was required in Sarajevo for the operation of hospitals, domestic purposes, and the operation of trams, came to Sarajevo via Buca Potok, that is the same substation referred to you by as Sarajevo 7; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And in exceptional circumstances, also came to Velesici in the direction of Vogosca. Those moments when the pylon between Visegrad and Vogosca were working, then that's when we directed the electricity. So Velesici was also used but the main transformer station was Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you be able to say, sir, if the main transformers at Buca Potok was the power or did not have power to distribute to Sarajevo, what would be the effect? What would have been the effect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If there was no electricity, then there would be a breakdown somewhere on the pylon between Reljevo and Buca Potok. We would go there to decide and would repair as soon as the damage was repaired, then there would be electricity at the transformer station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you misunderstood my question. My question was if Buca Potok did not have power to distribute to Sarajevo, what would have been the effect? Let me approach this in a different way: Sarajevo then would have suffered a complete blackout; isn't that the was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. There would be a blackout.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And even for trams to operate in Sarajevo, that wouldn't be sufficient in power, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. There wouldn't be any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The substation in Buca Potok was only a distribution point; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The transformer station of Buca Potok received electricity from Reljevo, and the distribution further on from Buca Potok was conducted by Electroprivreda of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they distributed as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's good. So the substation at Buca Potok was supplied with power from Reljevo, you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Reljevo was the only substation which provided or supplied power to Buca Potok?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever visited the Reljevo substation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to observe its control panel?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen the switch, or to use your terminology perhaps, the circular breaker which is listed as Buca Potok on that panel?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If that circular breaker was switched off, what would be the effect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That circular breaker, what would happen is that that would be detrimental for the city of Sarajevo. But that would be switched off only at the moment if the pylon would break down. Because the equipment, as we call it, we would then have to switch off the circular breaker to stop the electricity in the pylon, so that the workers wouldn't be harmed. After the repair was done, then they would following a message and instructions, we would then again switch off -- switch on the circular breaker for Buca Potok. If you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir my question was not when the circular breaker was switched off but as to the effect of switching off the circular breaker. What would happen if it was switched off?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: There would be no electricity in Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So Sarajevo would be subject to a complete blackout?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this applies to all the areas under -- in Sarajevo under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that there was the capability of the mere flick of a switch to subject the entire Sarajevo to a complete blackout from Reljevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, but this never happened, not once.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you or do you know as to who, which army, was in control of the territory in which the Reljevo substation was located?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, in your examination-in-chief, you stated that an officer of one of the armies could walk into a transformer unit or substation and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. make certain requests as to switch off power supplies to certain areas.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that in answer to a question with relation to the part of the city under the control of BH Army, that any of them could have gone in and asked for supply of one or other part of the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Likewise, in the circumstances, even members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had the capacity to walk into the substation in Reljevo and request that the circular breaker labelled "Buca Potok" -- pardon the pronunciation -- to be switched off?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that never happened, that they would go in and request that, demand that. Because we -- we were very careful about the behaviour of our people who were working in transformer station, that nobody would be able to have access to the switch, apart from the person who was technically in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If trams are to be operated, you essentially require power; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if any party wished trams to cease from operations, the best possible means to achieve this would be to ensure that the power supply to Sarajevo is terminated; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area, sir. You testified that during the period September 1992 to August 1994 you were employed as a professional technician, if I may use that word, to carry out repairs to power lines?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During this period, were you required to report on a daily basis to a particular duty station?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What kind of station do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have a particular duty station where you were required to report to daily?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I had a director of the company, and every day I would see it was in Vrelo Stanica station, every day we were located there and waited for the reports to come in. If some damage was done somewhere that very same moment we could set up and repair the damage. And the reports, I never had to submit any reports because just to say -- perhaps just to say this damage has been repaired and this pylon can now be switched on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So where were you instructed or who instructed you to carry out the repairs you were required to carry out?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no instructions that were issued. I would simply agree, myself, with my Muslim colleagues in terms on how we are going to carry out repairs. So we were the experts who had worked before the war together. We knew each other well. And we knew also how was one to carry out these repairs. So we would then agree what would be the easiest way of carrying out repairs with the agreement of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So how did you know when to carry out which repairs and where? Were you not instructed by some person?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: When the damage occurred, the electrician on duty at the transformer station between which and the other side of the transformer station where there was damage done, he would then inform us that the pylon wasn't working. So I would come out from my side up to the lines of the Republika Srpska Army, and my colleagues would arrive from the other side would come to the lines of the Army of BH, and we would then establish where the damage was done, where the breakdown occurred. So then we would agree on how to repair the damage, with the agreement of both armies, to ensure through UNPROFOR this peace while we repaired the damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So according to your testimony, sir, repairs were carried out in consultation with both the armies and through the mediation of UNPROFOR in most of the instances; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, as you stated, you said like on the side of the confrontation lines where you were working and living, on the other side, that is on the territory controlled by the BH Army, there was also professional technicians who were capable of carrying out repairs to power lines and pylons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In which instant, was there any necessity for a professional technician to ever cross the confrontation line and go on to the territory controlled by the opposing army to carry out repairs to power lines located in that territory?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That didn't happen once, but some hundreds of times my team went across the Muslim trenches, Muslim army trenches, and the other way around. Their team went to the area under the control of the Republika Srpska Army so that we would carry out the repair together. And for your information, for all the going out into the field to carry out repairs, we had to go across the territory under the control of Republika Srpska Army. So from Reljevo, Vogosca to the Zuc area where there was most repairs had to be carried out in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you and --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't understand, my team and the Muslim team, we both had to go into the field under the control of the Republika Srpska Army. So, from the Reljevo checkpoint through Vogosca to the Zuc elevation or from Reljevo direction to the Zuc area elevation point, depending which pylon wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position then that the repairs you carried out were on power lines located in territory controlled by the Republika Srpska Army, that is the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. There was damage between the demarcation lines of both armies, and we would come to repair that damage. Going via the territory controlled by the Republika Srpska Army, went across the trenches of Republika Srpska Army, carried out the repairs, and if there was need, we would go across the trenches of the BH Army if there was damage done to a pylon somewhere behind their lines. Myself, my people, and the team from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So why was it required for you and your team to cross the line and go into the trenches or the territory controlled by the BH Army when there were in fact professional technicians on that side of the line?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Because we didn't believe that all the people were normal over there, and if they said that someone wouldn't shoot, that's why we went together, that one Muslim and one Serb would go up on the pylon so that nobody would know, the army wouldn't know so they wouldn't shoot, who was who. I will give you one incident. In the area of Sabanova Kuca, we worked on the territory behind the BH Army lines. We didn't finish the job that day. When we went to withdraw, my colleague Sabanovic was asked by a soldier, "Where are you going Saban?" So he said, "I want to see off my Serbs from Ilidza, so that the next day, God willing, we can come and repair so that there is electricity in Sarajevo." This soldier said that he was cursing our Chetnik mother and that he would kill us, so that he took Saban into one of the houses and we had the problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could keep your answers short, because I am under time constraint. Now, when you --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. I had to tell you this, while we worked together, this happened because of this incident that a certain individual caused, not just for me but for others, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you said that when repairs were carried out it was done in consultation with both armies and on the mediation of UNPROFOR; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And generally at times when repairs were carried out at the repair site, the liaison officer of both the armies, together with members of UNPROFOR; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were present, the liaison officers of Electroprivreda Republika Srpska and of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Elektroprivreda, and very rarely liaison officers of the armies, of the representative armies, the Republika Srpska Army and BH Army, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Wasn't there procedure in place, sir, when UNPROFOR got involved in repairs to utilities where both -- liaison officers of both armies had to be present at the repair sites?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, only the officers were present at the moments when we had meetings or agreements on how we would carry out repairs at some critical points like Cakrcici and sometimes these elevation points in Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that Ilidza was deprived of power at certain times?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was the power -- the substation which supplied power to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The transformer station Blazuj and it got supply also from the Reljevo substation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know which army was -- which army controlled the territory in which the Blazuj substation was located?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you earlier stated that the territory on which the Reljevo substation was located was controlled by the Republika Srpska Army, that is the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which army controlled the territory Visegrad? Pardon the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that the hydroelectrical power plant in Jablanica, and the power plant in Kakanj, those territories were controlled by the BH Army? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, from those power sources in order to distribute power to Sarajevo and Ilidza and other areas, power had to be distributed via substations; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And power distributed to Sarajevo as you stated earlier from the substation in Reljevo which was under the control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And power is distributed to Ilidza through the substation in Blazuj which was also under the control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR RADOJEVIC
